newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy seeks bids for "cleansed" Banco di Napoli.
newsitem.headline: Italy seeks bids for "cleansed" Banco di Napoli.

text.p: Italy will launch the privatisation of Banco di Napoli next month, offering the market a healthy bank which has been cleansed of all its bad debts, Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Tuesday.
The Treasury said it would sell an initial 60 percent chunk of southern Italy's largest financial institution to the highest domestic or foreign bidder.

"Banco di Napoli is a clean bank, freed from the problems of old management," Ciampi told a news conference, adding that there were no further huge hidden losses lurking in the Italian banking system.

Potential buyers have until November 18 to declare an interest in the sale and will then be given until December 20 to make their final offer, although the Treasury is encouraging bidders to lay their cards on the table by December 2.
Banco di Napoli unveiled record losses of 3.12 trillion lire ($2.0 billion) in 1995 and plunged a further 674 billion lire into the red in the first half of this year.
New management was hastily installed and it rapidly launched a restructuring programme, selling non-core operations and reducing the bank's presence in the north of the country.

In addition the government has set up a special company, Reviban, to take over most of the Neapolitan group's poor or doubtful loans, much of which was handed out for political rather than economic reasons.

A Treasury official said the government would decide by mid-November how much bad debt Reviban would take on, but newspapers say around 12.3 trillion lire of doubtful loans would be removed from Banco di Napoli's books.
"Banco di Napoli will offer the sort of normality that perhaps no other bank can offer because it will be cleansed of these (bad) debts," Ciampi said.

The bank's sell-off is linked to a 2.28 trillion lire capital increase at the group, with the Treasury providing some 2.0 trillion lire of fresh funds to lift its stake from the present 13 percent to nearly 100 percent. At the moment a non-profit making foundation owns a majority stake in the bank.
A Treasury official hinted that the government wanted to get this money back from the privatisation but Ciampi declined to estimate how much he hoped the sale would raise.

Once the initial 60 percent holding is sold, Ciampi said that the Treasury would look to sell its remaining 40 percent stake swiftly. "We are holding onto the quota...for a limited period of time to allay any fears the clients might have about the bank's future," he said.

The Treasury has stipulated that only banks, insurance companies, financial and investment institutions can bid for Banco di Napoli. Interested companies must have made a profit in each of the last three years.
Until now only Banco Ambrosiano Veneto has expressed an interest in buying Banco di Napoli, but analysts believe Banca Commerciale Italiana is also interested.

So far no foreign group has shown any desire to get involved in the southern bank and analysts say investors abroad are wary of the Italian banking sector as a whole following years of persistent underperformance.
Ciampi admitted that domestic banks had suffered but said the worst was now past.
"The Italian banking system has not had an easy time but there's nothing (now) which can or should cause particular concern," he told reporters.
